analytic.title: Extended Level Real Time Scheduling Framework Using a Generalized Non-Real Time Platform

div.p: The feasible execution of real time tasks over a platform majorJy depends upon the scheduling policies to be used. Also, different task domains comply to different resource requirements. Allocating resources optimally according to the task requirements is a core challenge to the real time systems community. This paper discusses an approach where we leverage a generalized non-real time system to develop an integrated schedule for real time tasks by extending the control for resource allocation to the user level. A major advantage of this framework is that it does not involve any modifications to the underlying kernel code or the use of patches. In our framework, two levels of scheduling are maintained, where at the base level the task schedule is decided by the kernel internally, and at the extended level, the user determines a separate schedule. Both the schedules are maintained inside the kernel. Each schedule is preceded by a schedulability test which governs the feasibility of execution of the incoming task set.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The tendency towards the use of customized systems for real time requirements can directly be related to the desired perfonnance and reliability in tenns of meeting specified deadlines. These systems deploy specialized scheduling algorithms to derive an optimal schedule so as to maximize the utility of the system. Some of the platfonns fulfilling these requirements are RTLinux, FreeRTOS and QNX. These platfonns generally rely on specialized versions or patches which involve modifications of the existing kernel code. This may lead to inconsistency across kernel versions as patches get tied to specific kernel versions and hence different patches may be required while testing with different platfonns. Also, improperly designed patches may even introduce new problems into the system.

In our framework, we follow a patchless approach which leverages a generalized non-real time system to meet real time requirements and works as an extension to it. The framework inhibits any modifications to the underlying kernel.

978-1-4799-3080-7114/$31.00 ©2014 IEEE Through this framework, we also ensure that the variable resource requirements of the tasks are appropriately met as we allow the user to control the execution of these tasks.

The key idea is to maintain a virtual layer inside the kernel on top of the in-built scheduler. Figure 1 illustrates the proposed framework. Through this layer we address the issue of control over scheduling decisions as this layer allows the user to superimpose its execution requirements over the schedule decided by the system. Also, this extension is portable across different Linux platfonns as it makes minimal use of the in-built Linux functions. Further, user-defined scheduling algorithms can easily be added to this layer so that we can test and modify the order of execution of tasks depending on variable resource requirements. Another benefit of this system is that this extension can be easily removed from the system, which will provide a dual mode platfonn to the user i.e. the real time mode when the extension is activated and the non-real time mode when the extension is deactivated.

div.head: II. MOTIVATION AND RELATED WORK
div.p: The prime motivation towards our work is to develop a mechanism that would empower generalized non-real time systems like Linux to support real time applications with a controlled manner of execution. This approach will provide a flexible environment to the users for governing the allocation of CPU-time to the real time tasks depending on their requirements. Also, using a generalized platfonn would eliminate the costs of proprietary systems and special purpose hardware to support real time requirements. The aim is also to avoid changes to the underlying kernel source code so that the system can keep up with the updates in subsequent kernel versions without any compatibility issues.

There have been various research endeavors that relate to our work. As we primarily focus on extension rather than on modification, some previous works on extension for providing real time support include RT-UNIX [1], [2] and RT-MACH [2], [3], [4],[5], [6]. They represent the real time extensions of UNIX and MACH, respectively. These approaches make use of standard peripheral devices and interfaces that allow to speed up the execution of real time applications whereas our framework does not require any external hardware support. A major disadvantage of using such extensions is that the basic kernel mechanisms which may be inappropriate for handling real time tasks often remain preserved even in the real time version of the system. For example, most internal queues are handled with a FIFO policy and the same policy may also be used in real time situations which may ultimately degrade the perfonnance. Contrarily, in our framework we allow different scheduling policies based on the requirements of the tasks to be easily added to the existing platfonn.
Other relevant works include LITMUS RT [7] and SC HED _ DEADLINE [8] which are patch-based schedulers whereas our framework inhibits the use of patches.

Existing work [9],[ 1 0],[11 ], [12], [13], [ 14], [15] also includes implementations mostly targeted for Linux. These implementations remain specific to certain platfonns due to which translation across various platfonns becomes difficult whereas our framework is portable across different platfonns. RTLinux[ll] and Portable RK(Resource Kernel) [15] are also patch-based solutions that enhance the real time capabilities of Linux.

Another relevant work is "Hijack" [16] that enables commercial-off-the-shelf(COTS) systems with an execution environment and corresponding services, to support real time applications. They also avoid modifications to the underlying kernel by employing kernel modules which is similar to our work. But these modules are used to intercept kernel services to be further used by user space tasks whereas in our framework, we directly perfonn scheduling operations into the kernel module. Also, Hijack assumes the underlying architecture to be x86 whereas our implementation is hardware independent. Another platfonn independent solution is "ExSched" [17], which allows different schedulers to be developed for different operating systems(OS) without modifying the kernel. On the contrary, our framework adds a level of scheduling into the system which is controlled completely by the user. We have also added a schedulability criteria before the actual execution of the tasks in order to minimize the possibilities of deadline misses. Another implementation [20] allows both real time and non-real time tasks to be executed on the same platfonn which is similar to our work. This implementation makes the use of open off-the shelf machines and networks. For scheduling support they also have their implementations in the context of MidART [18], [ 19], a real time network middleware.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume that the framework allows admission of new tasks at any instant of time which can be periodic or sporadic in nature. A listener is maintained inside the framework which keeps track of arrival of all the tasks. Each task Tj is characterized by a four tuple (Cj , Dj , Pj , Prj), where Cj denotes the worst-case computation time, Dj denotes the relative deadline, Pj denotes the period in case of periodic tasks and minimum inter-arrival time in case of sporadic tasks, and Prj denotes the priority of the task. We particularly assume constrained-deadline systems which satisfy the condition Cj :S Dj :S Pj for any Tj so as to minimize the possibility of preemption of two or more instances of the same task by each other.
The submitted tasks also undergo a schedulability test corresponding to the scheduling policy selected by the user.

div.head: IV. FRAMEWORK DESCRIPTION
div.p: This section presents a complete description of the framework including both the user and the system controlled levels.

The framework aims to provide a real time support to a generalized non-real time system with an additive control of the user to manipulate the scheduling decisions of the submitted tasks. We achieve this without making any modifications to the underlying OS kernel or using any patches.
For the feasible execution of these real time tasks, we follow an integrated scheduling approach by dividing the scheduling responsibility into two levels -extended level and base level.

div.head: A. Extended Level
div.p: In the extended level of scheduling, we introduce a virtual layer to be sandwiched between the user application submitting real time tasks and the underlying OS scheduler(which is at the base level). This layer contains a loadable kernel module which can be dynamically loaded and unloaded to and from the kernel. This kernel module is responsible for associating timing properties to the existing task structure. It also includes all the relevant components corresponding to the scheduling of tasks. Table I shows the basic scheduling components that are used at the extended level of scheduling. Figure 3 illustrates the core scheduling components and handling of tasks by these components inside the framework. Also, this kernel module is extensible in nature as new scheduling policies can easily be added to it in the form of library functions.

The components inside the rt_sched module coordinate together to derive a primary schedule at this level. This schedule is significant to determine the priority order for the real time tasks present at this level. This primary schedule utterly depends upon the scheduling policy to be implemented which further is selected by the user according to the task requirements. The interaction between the user application and the rt_sched module for selection of scheduling policy is conducted with the help of ioctiO system call. For this, we build the module as a character device module which can be accessed through the device file /dev/rt _ sched.
The system can return to the general non-real time mode by unloading the rt_ sched module from the kernel.

div.head: B. Base Level
div.p: The base level refers to the in-built scheduler operability inside the underlying non-real time OS. Since the primary aim of our framework is to inhibit any modifications to the existing kernel, we only import the real time tasks derived from the primary schedule (at the extended level) to be executed by the system at the base level. At this level, again a scheduling policy (which maybe SC HED JIFO or SC HED _ RR) [20] is selected and a secondary schedule is maintained internal to the system. The actual execution of the task gets initiated at this level.

The assignment of static priority for the real time tasks is vital, as at this level the imported real time task competes for resources with other non-real time tasks co-existing in the system. The static priority of the task can be assigned by using the sched_setparam(pid , sched�aram) function.

Both the levels maintain a continuous connection with each other in order to keep track of interrupts in the form of newly arrived jobs or during job termination. The importance of a schedulability test is to anticipate the feasible execution of the task set submitted as input. The failure to this test indicates the possibility of partial execution of some or all of the tasks till they reach their respective deadlines. This leads to strategic conditions in case of safety critical tasks and declined task utility otherwise [21]. In our framework, we allow the execution of only those tasks that satisfy the schedulability test.

Our framework allows the user to implement different scheduling policies at the extended level. Corresponding to each scheduling policy there exists a separate schedulability test. At the initial stage, we follow a global schedulability test according to which the total utilization of the set of submitted tasks must be less than 1.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL DEMONSTRA nON
div.p: This section includes the sample implementation with the framework attached to a generalized non-real time system.

div.head: A. Experimental Setup
div.p: For our prototype implementation, we have used Linux kernel version 3.8.0-35 with 64-bit Intel based architecture. The framework supports both single and multi-core architectures and is portable across various kernel versions with either slight or no modification in the rt_ sched module as this module makes minimal use of the functions imported by the Linux kernel. Also, in terms of non-real time tasks, we have allowed several foreground and background processes to co-exist while the module is loaded into the kernel.

div.head: B. Two-Level Scheduling Demonstration
div.p: This section elaborates the handling of real time tasks within our framework taking a sample task set with specified parameters. Table IV illustrates the parameters assigned to the task set. Figure 5 & 6 show the corresponding Gantt Chart for execution of the sample task set. Since in our implementation, we have extended the scheduling at two levels, we observe that the Gantt chart includes both the real time and the non-real time tasks each competing for processor time. Due to the assignment of lower values of static pnonty (lower values indicate higher priority), the incoming real time tasks from the extended level can interrupt the execution of the currently executing non-real time tasks at the base level. The time when no task remains to be scheduled at the extended level (waiting for the arrival of any new instance or during termination), other non-real time tasks (present in the waitqueue) are allocated processor time. Also, the core components while discussing scheduling include the dispatcher and the scheduler which are required at the time of each task switch or new task arrival. For each context switch at the extended level, both the primary and the secondary schedules are affected. Hence, at each scheduling point, we use both the extended and the base level scheduling components. In the Gantt chart shown in Figure 5 & 6, we have highlighted the scheduling points with dotted lines.

div.head: C. Result
div.p: The framework allows feasible execution of the real time tasks on the non-real time platform. It has been observed that the tasks almost never missed their deadlines as at the extended level the filtering is done by the schedulability test after which either the task set is discarded or according to the primary schedule the real time tasks are passed to the base level. At the base level, the incoming real time tasks carrying a lower value of static priority(lower values indicate higher priority) either interrupt a majority of tasks already present at the base level runqueue or lead to the migration of the tasks to other available cores(if any).
Using our framework, we have also increased the processor demand of the system thereby augmenting the performance of the system as a whole.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Through this paper, we presented an Extended Level Real time Scheduling Framework which supports additive control of user towards the scheduling decisions of tasks. The introduction of the virtual layer to the underlying OS was done without modifying the base kernel which adds to its portability.

The core component of this layer was the rt_sched module which includes the various scheduling policies according to the user requirements. This module is extensible in nature which allows the user to add further policies to be implemented. Another benefit of this framework is that it can be easily loaded and unloaded to and from the kernel thereby providing a dual mode platform to the users. Although similar works have been done earlier but our approach is different in terms of providing the user with the liberty to make scheduling decisions through the extended level. We have also focused on ensuring the correctness and performance of our model by necessitating schedulability tests for all the task sets.

A limitation to our work includes the verification of the rt_ sched module for minor changes in case of different kernel versions. Also, in our schedulability test, we have considered the utilization to be maximum 100% in both the uniprocessing and multiprocessing environment whereas in case of multiple cores we can take a higher value of utilization.
The future work may include implementation of the framework on other platforms like Windows and Android.
